+| 4   | **Depth = scene nesting**; within a scene one flat coordinate space                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             | Containment is the hierarchy; grouping inside a scene is visual only.                                                                                                                  |

+- **Drill-in** = animate the camera to fit the portal (`interpolateZoom`, 250–800 ms), then swap the root scene
+  and re-express the camera in child space (`enterPortal`); **drill-out** is the inverse (`exitPortal`) followed
+  by a fit of the parent. Both verified seamless in the spike.
+- **Auto drill**: after a zoom gesture settles (150 ms), a portal covering ≥ 85% of the viewport becomes the root;
+  a root covering < 30% yields to its parent. The swap preserves coverage, so the two rules cannot oscillate.
+- **Tiers** for a portal by on-screen size (`min(size) × composed zoom`): `< 40px` tile, `< 260px` title +
+  cell count (later: rasterised thumbnail), else live child scene, only while `depth < 2`. Hysteresis of ±10% at
+  the boundaries.
+
+## 6. Navigation
+
+| Gesture                                                                | Effect                                                                       |
+| ---------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| Double-click a portal, or Enter with a portal selected                 | Animated drill-in                                                            |
+| Pinch/ctrl+wheel until a portal fills the view                         | Auto drill-in (no animation, camera preserved)                               |
+| Escape, breadcrumb click, "Up", or zooming the root below 30% coverage | Drill-out (breadcrumb jumps several levels)                                  |
+| Alt+← / Alt+→                                                          | Back / forward through a history of `{path, camera}` entries                 |
+| Shift+1 / Shift+2 / Shift+0                                            | Fit scene / fit selection / reset zoom                                       |
+| Double-click a non-portal cell                                         | Opens it (`CellDef.openable`, e.g. text editing, or the ECHO object)         |
+| URL / deep link (phase 3)                                              | `{path, camera}` serialised so a location inside a nested scene is shareable |
+
+## 6b. Mobile navigation mode
+
+The 2D camera is replaced, not shrunk. Below the `md` breakpoint or when the primary input is coarse
+(`(pointer: coarse) and (hover: none)`), and always when the host asks for it (`mode='columns'`), `SceneView`
+renders the current scene as **columns**: a horizontally paged strip of full-height panels, one per **aspect**.
+The `columns` mode reads the same positioned `Scene` from the same `Projection`; it adds no model state.
+
+**Aspect** = a named, ordered, read-only projection of one scene into a vertical list. The engine ships these
+and a `CellDef` may contribute more (`CellDef.aspects?: (cell) => Aspect[]`):
+
+| Aspect         | Column contents                                                                                                                           | Order                                                                                                  |
+| -------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
+| `overview`     | every placed cell as a row (kind icon, label, summary); portals are rows that open the child scene as the next column                     | layout order: top-to-bottom, then left-to-right by cell centre, so a diagram reads the way it is drawn |
+| `cells:<kind>` | one column per cell kind present in the scene (rects, text, objects, portals)                                                             | same                                                                                                   |
+| `links`        | every link as `source → target` with its label; tapping either end selects that cell and scrolls `overview` to it                         | by source row, then target row                                                                         |
+| `cell:<id>`    | the selected cell in detail: its full content (`Surface` for object cells, the editor for text), its ports, and its links grouped by port | pushed when a row is tapped; one per selected cell                                                     |
+| `scene:<path>` | a nested scene, i.e. the `overview` of the child, reached from a portal row                                                               | pushed on drill-in                                                                                     |
+
+Aspects form a **strip** `Aspect[]`; the view keeps `{path, strip, column}` in the per-view atoms next to the
+2D `{path, camera}` and both survive a mode switch, so rotating a phone or docking a tablet moves between the
+2D camera and the column the user was reading (the column's first visible row maps to a camera fit on that
+cell; a camera maps to the `overview` column scrolled to the first fully visible cell).
+
+Navigation:
+
+| Gesture                                                               | Effect                                                                                                                                             |
+| --------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| Horizontal swipe, or the tab bar above the strip                      | Previous / next column in the strip                                                                                                                |
+| Tap a row                                                             | Push a `cell:<id>` column after the current one and page to it; selection follows                                                                  |
+| Tap a portal row, or the "open" affordance on a `scene` row           | Drill-in: push `scene:<path>` (its `overview`); the breadcrumb grows                                                                               |
+| Back (swipe from the edge, breadcrumb tap, hardware back via history) | Pop the pushed columns to that point; drill-out is popping past a `scene:` column                                                                  |
+| Long-press a row                                                      | Context menu: open, select, delete (the same intents as §8)                                                                                        |
+| Reorder rows by drag (`overview` and `cells:` only)                   | A `move` intent that keeps the cell's x and moves it to the dropped neighbour's y; the projection decides what it means, exactly as on the 2D view |

Cancelled gestures are covered by 444ea390 and d3cbf328: Escape, a palette drag leaving the canvas and now `pointercancel` all go through `cancelDrag`, which drops the pending node with the drag, so nothing is committed and the next gesture calls `create` afresh. body:
Cast is gone, `533e84d`. `serveOnRouter` no longer erases the group: it declares the served group's codec requirement (`Rpc.ServicesServer<Served<Rpcs>>`, `never` for every concrete group), and `RpcRouter.ServeOptions` now types a registration's in-process client by its own rpcs, so `RegisterService` passes `makeInProcessClient(rpc, handlers)` with no assertion.

What is left is one stated equality, in `handlerLayer`: `Rpc.ToHandler<R>` is `Handler<_Tag>` and `AddMiddleware` preserves `_Tag`, so `ToHandler<Rpcs>` and `ToHandler<Served<Rpcs>>` are the same services — but TypeScript cannot reduce `AddMiddleware` through a generic parameter, so it has to be asserted once in that helper rather than inferred.

The way to have none at all is for the timing middleware to be part of the rpc definitions (`RpcGroup.make(...).prefix('X.').middleware(RpcTiming.Middleware)`), so group, `Handlers`, `Client`, server and router all carry it and nothing is wrapped at serve time — which is what `requiredForClient` implies anyway. It needs `RpcTiming.Middleware` moved out of `@dxos/worker-framework` (which does not depend on `@dxos/protocols`) into `@dxos/protocols`; the metrics/log half of `RpcTiming` can stay where it is. Happy to do it here or as a follow-up — say which.

Also dissolved `withRpc` per your other note: the registrations are one `mergeAll` over the handler layers beneath them, and I kept the five your WIP list dropped (Data/Query/Feed/Logging/DevtoolsHost) plus fixed `Layer.provideMerge(RpcRouter.RpcRouter)`, which was passing the tag where a layer goes.

Correct and worth catching — `channel.close()` alone left the liveness-lock callback awaiting `livenessLockHeld` forever, so a displaced queued worker kept holding `${storageLockKey}/liveness/…`. Clients watch that key to detect termination, so the very worker that stood down would have continued to read as alive; `endpoint.close?.()` was also skipped. Now routed through `await shutdown()`, which releases both locks and closes the endpoint.

author: dmaretskyi
body:
No — displacement is purely cooperative, and you've put your finger on its limit.

**What happens today.** The displaced worker has to be running its event loop to hear the `BroadcastChannel` message and run `shutdown()`. Hard termination exists but lives on the other side: only the tab holding the `Worker` handle can call it, in `LeaderSession.#closeWorker()` → `this.#worker.terminate()` (`Client.ts:777`), reached from `_close()` or a failed handshake.

Those two do chain, for a *responsive* worker: `shutdown()` releases the liveness lock → the ex-leader tab's `navigator.locks.request(livenessLockKey, …)` callback fires (`Client.ts:735`) → `onClose.emit('Dedicated worker terminated.')` → the connection's handler (`Client.ts:315`) drops the session → `_close()` → `terminate()`. So in the orderly case the tab does terminate its worker; it just does so *after* and *because of* the cooperative shutdown.

**Which means the stuck case is exactly the gap.** A worker wedged badly enough not to service the channel never runs `shutdown()`, never releases the liveness lock, so its tab is never told anything is wrong and never reaches `terminate()`. The new worker cannot terminate it either — cross-worker there is no handle, only the channel it is already ignoring. It keeps the storage lock, and we are back to the 15s budget.

**So your suggestion is the right next step, with one caveat.** Having the spawning tab terminate on displacement covers a genuinely different failure class from this PR: the worker is wedged but *its tab is alive*. It does not help when the tab itself is gone or saturated — which is the case this PR addresses, and why worker-to-worker displacement had to work at all.

Concretely it would need a tab-side signal that does not depend on the wedged worker: the displacing worker broadcasts, and the ex-leader **tab** (not its worker) hears it and calls `terminate()`. That needs a channel the tab listens on, plus a decision about how long to wait for a graceful shutdown before terminating — terminating immediately would cut off a worker that was merely slow, mid-flush.

Happy to do it, but it is a design change beyond this PR's scope rather than a fix to it, and this PR is green as it stands. Two options:

1. Land this, and I open a follow-up issue for tab-side termination on displacement.
2. I extend this PR with it now.

Your call — tell me which and I'll do it.

Agreed, and removed in `c51c175e`.

It was a compatibility re-export left behind when `displaceChannelFor` moved to `./internal/displace-channel.ts` — exactly what CLAUDE.md forbids: *"Never leave compatibility re-exports or shims when moving code. Update every call site to the new location in the same change."*

It was also dead. The only uses of `displaceChannelFor` are inside `Worker.ts` itself (the `displace()` default and `run()`'s `displaceChannel` default), both of which already import it directly from `./internal/displace-channel.ts` on line 19. Nothing outside the package referenced `Worker.displaceChannelFor` — `@dxos/worker-framework/Worker` is imported by `client/src/services/dedicated/dedicated-worker.ts`, `client/src/testing/storage-lock.ts` and the counter story, and none of them touch it.

So the line re-exported a symbol nobody imported, purely to paper over the move. Deleted rather than plumbed through `index.ts`: if a consumer ever needs the channel name, it should be exported deliberately, not inherited from a shim.

Verified after removal: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `worker-framework:test` 39/39, `worker-framework:test-browser` 43/43, `client:test` 42 passed, lint clean.

body:
Real, and fixed in `1c3aafe3` — though not the way the finding suggests. Plumbing a terminal/transient distinction out of the transport would mean threading HTTP status through `Control`, which pipes everything through `Effect.orDie` by design; that is a bigger change than this PR should carry.

Instead the flusher now caps attempts (`DEFAULT_MAX_ATTEMPTS = 12`, configurable). Past the cap the command and its process's group are purged and the process is reported `FAILED` rather than dropped in silence, so one poison command can no longer hold every later command — for every other process — behind it. At the default backoff the cap is hours away, so an outage never reaches it; a persistent rejection does.

Covered by a new e2e case: a doomed spawn queued ahead of a second one, asserting the second still gets through and the first reads `FAILED`.

author: dmaretskyi
body:
You're right about the ceiling and I was wrong — corrected in `928e287e`.

I claimed the cap was "hours away" without doing the arithmetic. It isn't: with `initial: 1s, max: 60s`, twelve attempts is `1+2+4+8+16+32+60×5 ≈ 363s`, six minutes. An ordinary offline stretch would have discarded commands the user asked for, which is exactly the durability violation you named.

The give-up point is now **elapsed time since the command first failed** (`DEFAULT_GIVE_UP_AFTER = 24h`, configurable), pinned via a new `firstFailedAt` on the queue record. A closed laptop, a flight, an edge deploy — none come close; a command the host keeps rejecting still stops holding the ordered queue behind it. Counting attempts was measuring elapsed time with the units filed off, since the backoff caps out.

On your other objection — dropping only the current command and leaving its siblings retrying — that one doesn't apply: the branch calls `queue.purgeProcess(command.localPid)`, so the whole group goes, and the process is reported `FAILED`.

I'm not plumbing a terminal/transient classification out of the transport in this PR. `Control` carries no error channel by design (`EdgeProcessControl` is `Effect.orDie` throughout), so threading HTTP status through it is a change to that contract and belongs on its own. The time horizon is the conservative stand-in: it cannot fire on an outage, and it bounds the wedge.

author: dmaretskyi
body:
Both findings on this hunk are fixed in `0634ea31`.

**Targeting (major).** Confirmed: `BroadcastChannel` delivers to every tab on the storage lock and the self-check skips only the issuer, so with an incumbent plus two other tabs the two bystanders kill their own workers — contradicting F-3.5 and over-reporting `WorkerTerminationError` to telemetry.

Carrying an incumbent id in the request does not work here: the issuer is a *queued* worker, and nothing tells it who holds the storage lock (`navigator.locks.query()` exposes lock names and UA-generated client ids, never our `workerId`). So the decision is taken locally, by each tab, from two facts it can establish about its own worker:

1. **Its liveness lock is still held.** `Worker.run` takes that lock inside the storage-lock grant and releases it in the same `shutdown()`, so the two have identical lifetimes — a worker that already stood down is neither killed again nor reported.
2. **It does not answer a `ping`** within `LeaderTimeouts.workerProbeTimeout` (default 1s, injectable). Answering is what a worker servicing its event loop does, and not servicing it is exactly why the lock is still held.

For 3+ tabs that is sound without knowing the incumbent's id: every healthy bystander answers its probe and stands down, so at most one worker — the wedged one — is terminated, however many tabs listen. The issuer self-check is kept, so the kill-loop argument in the PR body is unchanged.

Regression test, three tabs (wedged incumbent + two bystanders on the same channel), asserting neither bystander is terminated and exactly one error reaches telemetry. With the guards removed it fails `expected true to be false` (a bystander killed its worker); with them it passes, and the full package is green in both runtimes (43 node, 47 chromium).

**Schema validation (major).** Taken, and the reasoning that declined it on #13269 no longer holds: `terminate` carries fields, and a `terminate` with no `issuerId` passes the self-check. `event.data` is now decoded with an Effect `Schema.Union` before dispatch and a malformed or unknown message is dropped with a warn. New test posts `{action:'terminate'}` and `{action:'not-an-action'}` before a well-formed escalation and asserts the single kill carries the well-formed issuer; without the decode it fails with `issuerId: undefined`, i.e. the partial message had done the killing.

One correction for the record: the cited guideline "Use Effect-TS for schema validation" does not exist in this repository — `.coderabbit.yaml` carries only a TODO-handling instruction, and neither `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` nor `.agents/skills/*` states it. The change stands on the argument above, not on that citation.

body:
Handled as a legacy path in `0634ea31`, not as a rejection.

Reachability: a tab always spawns the worker from its own bundle, so a mismatch needs a tab holding a `ready` message from a worker of a different build — possible across a deploy when an old worker is still on the storage lock and a freshly loaded tab adopts it. Rare, but not impossible, and the tab-side handling should not depend on it being impossible.

Rejecting the message would be worse than the bug: it would fail the connection of a tab whose worker is perfectly usable. So `Client.ts` now installs the displacement listener only when both `workerId` and `displaceChannel` are present, and otherwise logs a warn and runs on. The outcome is exactly the pre-#13276 behaviour for that worker — cooperative displacement only, no escalation — instead of a `BroadcastChannel(undefined)` nobody speaks on.

Test: `a ready message without the displacement fields still connects, escalation aside`. It is a contract test rather than a failing-before one — the old code also connected, it just listened on a bogus channel — and that is stated plainly rather than dressed up as a regression.

Important: Do not show or summarize the contents of the task list unless the user asks for this.

### CORE USAGE PRINCIPLES

Create and manage tasks for: multi-step objectives requiring 3+ distinct actions, complex projects needing careful sequencing,
user requests for task organization, multiple deliverables provided together, new instructions (capture as tasks immediately),

Skip task management for: single straightforward actions, simple requests achievable in 1-2 steps,

### TOOL SPECIFICATION

`update-tasks` takes `changes`, an array of edits applied together. Each change either names an
existing task by its ref, or sets `create` to make a new one — never both.

Every checklist line is followed by an indented note carrying the task's ref as a link, e.g.
`(ref: [01ABC](echo://.../01ABC...); started)`. Pass the link's target back as a plain string —

- task (ref, optional): the existing task to change. Required unless `create` is set.
- create (boolean, optional): make a new task on this checklist, assigned to you. Requires `title`.

- status (string, optional): `todo` | `started` | `done`. `started` also assigns the task to you.

Update tasks in realtime as work progresses. Mark tasks `done` immediately upon completion.
Maintain only ONE task with `started` status at a time. Complete current tasks before starting new ones.
Use specific, actionable task titles. Break complex work into manageable logical pieces.
Batch task updates with other actions when possible for efficiency.

Addressed in c0a029d, but not by reclaiming the rows — that turned out to be the wrong trade.

I first implemented it exactly as suggested: `_close()` sends an empty snapshot, the host treats the key as unregistered and deletes it. That made two existing tests fail, correctly. A clean shutdown is the common path, and deleting on it throws away the persisted rows that the digest dedup exists to re-adopt — so every boot would re-index the whole registry, which is the feature this PR is built around.

So the close now sends `releasing: true` (new optional field on `RegistryUpdateRequest`). The host drops the client's ownership — which is the actual bug you identified, a closed client counting as a phantom owner forever — but keeps the rows. They are a cache; the next host session's first-push reconciliation reclaims whatever no client comes back for, which is the mechanism already in place.

Covered by `a client that closes stops counting as an owner`: after the close the row survives, and the remaining client's unregister then reclaims it — which it could not have done with a phantom owner still holding the key.

Addressed in ee11671, by removing the premise rather than retrying.

The gap was real but its cause was narrower than "the release failed": the client id was minted by the publisher, so a reopened client came back as a stranger and could never replace its own prior claim. The id now lives on `EchoClient` for the client's whole lifetime, so a reopen publishes under the same id and its first snapshot replaces the contribution the previous session filed.

Connection-scoped ownership would be stronger, but this RPC has no connection identity to hang it on (in-process clients, no per-connection teardown hook); that is a protocol change rather than something to fold in here.

body:
Fixed in `243cbb45`, though not by throwing — the diagnosis was right and the remedy needed to differ.

Each CDP step is now checked individually (`requestMemoryDump`, `Tracing.end`, and whether the completion actually won its race against the 10 s timeout), so a collection that did not happen returns empty instead of falling through to a parse of zero events. What it does **not** do is throw, because `StageRunner` catches a throwing collector into `ok: false`, and `toPosthogEvent` then refuses the whole row — one failed memory dump would discard that stage's wall time, CPU, thread, network, disk, RPC and lag readings, all of which were collected successfully. That trades a wrong memory number for eleven missing ones.

Instead the row carries `footprintProcesses`, and `appFootprintBytes: 0` with `footprintProcesses: 0` is unambiguous: nothing was collected. This is the idiom the harness already uses for exactly this class of problem — `sqliteRealms` for disk I/O, `wasmRealms` for wasm, `lagSamples*` for the drift probe — each one added because a zero and an absence read identically from the byte counters alone. `METRICS.md` documents it alongside them, and `report.test.ts` asserts that a failed read is distinguishable from an app holding no memory.

The property your finding asks for holds: a degraded collection cannot enter the trend as a valid measurement, because the integrity column marks it and the dashboard filters on it — the same way the SQLite tiles already filter on `ciSqliteRealms > 0`.

Because they measure rather than assert, and the two want opposite things from CI.

`startup.spec.ts` and `perf-*.spec.ts` don't pass or fail on behaviour — they record numbers (`appendRunSample`, `appendBenchmarkRow`, `writeReport`) that a separate gate then judges: `check-startup-budget` re-runs the warm-cold scenario with `--repeat-each=5` and gates on the **median**, and the perf nightly tracks the series. That's why they stayed behind: they're coupled to the build and the runner, not to the app's behaviour. `e2e-dev` needs `vite serve` rather than a bundle, and `e2e-welcome-focus` drives Storybook, so neither can run under the `composer-e2e` config at all.

Keeping them out is what lets the behavioural tier gate a merge. A timing test on a shared CI runner is flaky by construction, which is exactly why `check-startup-budget` is still manual — one of those in the gated suite and the pass/fail signal stops meaning anything.

On tracking them over time: yes, worth it, and I'd argue they deserve **their own** trend rather than a slot in this one. The stacked chart counts pass/fail/skip; a startup measurement has no such outcome — what you want plotted is milliseconds and module counts with a budget line, which is a different tile and a different event shape (`ci.e2e-test` has `ciStatus`/`ciDurationMs`, not `modulesAtReady`). The publisher is generic — `scripts/ci-event.mjs` already carries every other CI trend in the repo — so it's a small follow-up: emit `ci.startup` from the existing report and add a tile. Happy to do it in a follow-up PR; I don't think it should widen this one, since it needs its own event contract to be worth anything.

**Migrated — byte-for-byte identical, no output change:**

| site | was |
|---|---|
| `compute/nlp/src/hash.ts` | FNV-1a 32 → `fnv1a32(text).toString(16).padStart(8, '0')` |
| `compute/pipeline-rdf/…/reconcile.ts` | FNV-1a 32, carried a `TODO(burdon): Move to @dxos/util` |
| `compute/assistant-e2e/src/harness.ts` | private `fnv1a` |
| `plugin-studio/…/provider-options-cache.ts` | private `fingerprint` |
| `plugin-studio/…/mock-provider-plugin.ts` | private `hashPrompt` |
| `common/util/src/to-fallback.ts` | private `fnv1a` |
| `index-core` `contentHash` | inline 64-bit FNV-1a → `fnv1a64` |

`to-fallback.ts` needed care: its fold was `Math.abs` of the **signed** digest, which disagrees with an unsigned one for every input whose top bit is set. Those hues have shipped, so the fold is preserved exactly rather than quietly recolouring half the ids:

```ts
const paletteSeed = (id: string): number => Math.abs(fnv1a32(id) | 0);
```

**Left alone, with reasons:**

1. `common/keys/src/entity-id.ts` — two rotated lanes, not a duplicate of a one-lane hash.
2. `compute/ai/…/LanguageModelFixture.ts` — its `*31` hash is written into `<sanitized N>` inside stored fixtures; changing it invalidates them.
3. `react-ui-card/src/util.ts`, `react-ui-experimental/…/ghost-renderer.tsx`, `plugin-review/src/util/message.ts` — djb2 and `*31`. Swapping these is an algorithm change, not a consolidation: all three seed avatar/visual fallbacks, so existing names would get different colours. Happy to convert them if you want one algorithm across the board — just say and I'll do it in a follow-up rather than bury a palette change in this PR.

The `fnv1a64` width is deliberate where a collision means a *missed* difference rather than a shared bucket: 32 bits starts colliding around a few tens of thousands of inputs, which a content digest over a registry can reach. The test asserts 20k distinct inputs give 20k distinct digests.

`util` 139 passed, and every migrated package is green (`nlp` 22, `pipeline-rdf` 63, `plugin-studio` 19, `index-core` 65).

Correct, and my docs were overclaiming — fixed in `a92dcbc1`.

The check is **referential, not semantic**: it proves the two sides name each other and that the named test actually runs. It cannot read a spec and decide whether it exercises the flow's `steps`, and a test tagged `@QA-1` that asserts nothing passes it clean. `qa.mdl` said "coverage is a claim about the `steps`", which reads as if that claim were verified; it isn't, and both it and `BEST-PRACTICES.md` now say so and put the judgement on the reviewer.

Worth separating the two arms, because the behaviour *is* checked against the spec — just not by this link:

- The flow's steps carry `invoke:` and `assert:` (`assert: return $snapshot.spaces.some(…)`), and the `composer-qa` skill executes them against a live app, judging each step by the UI snapshot. That's the arm where the spec's prose is actually executed and where its assertions have teeth.
- The Playwright spec is the unattended arm — it runs on every CI cell, and what it asserts is whatever it was written to assert.

Nothing cross-checks those two against each other, and short of deriving one from the other I don't think anything can — which lands back on your original question. I'd argue that's the honest boundary rather than a gap to close: the value on offer is that every test points at a documented intent and the pointer can't rot silently, not that the pointer is proof of coverage.

One correction to my previous reply: I said nothing defines who writes which side first, and that was wrong — `BEST-PRACTICES.md` §1 already says **"Write the flow first"**, with the reasoning. What's genuinely undefined is the update path when a test legitimately changes shape, which is the part I'd still be happy to write down before landing if you want it.

+# Walkthrough eval results
+
+Four prompt variants, four real pull requests, scored two ways: a deterministic grader over the
+patch, and a blind LLM judge on the rubric in `docs/WALKTHROUGH-EVALS.md`. Every artefact is in the
+repository — prompts under `evals/prompts/`, the corpus and its generated documents under

+
+## What was measured
+
+| Variant        | What it adds                                                                                                         |
+| -------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
+| `v1-baseline`  | The prompt as it was before this work: structure, empty fences, "explain why".                                       |
+| `v2-readable`  | Plus the reader rules: one idea per sentence, mechanism not feeling, active voice, plain words, no em dash.          |
+| `v3-selective` | Plus: fence a repeated mechanical change once, every fence earns a paragraph, open each section with the constraint. |

Confirmed on all three points, and fixed in a commit not yet pushed (pushing right after this).

`_loadLinkedObjects` calls `_bindObjectDocument` *before* `_loadHandleForObject`, so after an unavailable verdict the object stays in `_objectDocumentHandles` — and both `_loadObjectDocument` (the `.has(objectId)` guard) and `_loadLinkedObjects` (the same-url guard) then short-circuit, so nothing restarts the load. And the `diskOnly` branch's detached `whenReady()` was a real regression from this PR: `_markUnavailable` rejects `_ready`, so the wait that used to stay pending under `requesting` now rejects at once and its `.catch` logs the recovery away.

I took a variant of your fix rather than the `change` listener: `_integrateHostUpdate` returns before emitting when the delivered bytes produce no patches, so a document that settles empty would deliver silently and never recover. `DocHandleProxy` now emits a dedicated `available` event on the `'unavailable' → 'ready'` transition only, and `#recoverWhenAvailable` arms a one-shot listener guarded exactly as you describe — `#isStale(generation)` plus `_objectDocumentHandles.get(objectId) === handle` — at both sites (the `DocumentUnavailableError` catch and the `diskOnly` branch).

const typeOnly = (members) =>

+# `@dxos/client-services` — restructure proposal
+
+Companion to [`DEPENDENCY-GRAPH.md`](./DEPENDENCY-GRAPH.md), which measures the
+current shape. This file proposes the target and the order to get there.
+
+## Goal
+
+1. **Acyclic.** `scripts/dependency-graph.mjs --check` exits 0.
+2. **Namespace modules.** Every module is `src/<Name>.ts`, marked
+   `@import-as-namespace`, re-exported as `export * as <Name>` from `index.ts`,
+   per the `code-style` skill (`@dxos/echo` is the reference).
+3. **Each module owns its wiring.** A module exports its own `Layer` _and_ its
+   own `LayerSpec`. `ServiceStack` assembles a list of specs; it does not
+   construct layers.
+4. **Minimal cross-deps.** A module imports a peer's _tag_, never its
+   implementation module.
+
+## Target layout
+
+```
+src/
+  index.ts                 -- export * as Foo from './Foo.ts'
+  errors.ts
+  Tags.ts                  -- every Context tag + its interface type   (tier 0)
+  Events.ts                -- lifecycle Hooks                          (tier 0)
+  Readiness.ts             -- StackReadiness                           (tier 0)
+  SqliteStorage.ts                                                     (tier 0)
+  Platform.ts                                                          (tier 0)
+  Migrations.ts                                                        (tier 0)
+
+  Metadata.ts  Pipeline.ts  SpaceExport.ts  Storage.ts                 (tier 1)
+  Replication.ts           -- EdgeFeedReplicator, credentials document (tier 1)
+  Auth.ts                  -- createAuthProvider, TrustedKeySet…       (tier 1)
+  Identity.ts              -- the Identity aggregate only              (tier 1)
+
+  IdentityManager.ts  Space.ts  Spaces.ts  Invitations.ts              (tier 2)
+  Devices.ts  Devtools.ts  Diagnostics.ts  Agents.ts
+  Logging.ts  Network.ts  System.ts
+
+  ServiceStack.ts          -- spec list + layerClientServices          (tier 3)
+  Worker.ts                                                            (tier 3)
+  testing/
+  internal/                -- not exported
+```
+
+Tier rule: a module may import strictly lower tiers only. `Tags.ts` imports
+nothing from the package.
+
+## Why `Tags.ts` rather than a tag per module
+
+The measurement in §2.2 of the graph doc is the argument: 3 of the 4 residual
+domain cycles exist because declaring a dependency on a peer requires importing
+that peer's implementation. Effect's own guidance is that a tag is an _interface_
+— putting the 18 tags plus their interface types in one leaf makes "module A
+depends on service B" expressible without an implementation edge, and is what
+takes the graph from a 2-cycle to acyclic.
+
+`Tags.ts` stays cheap because it holds interfaces and `Context.Service` classes
+only; every class body stays in its own module.
+
+## Stages
+
+Each stage is independently landable and leaves the build green.

+| `services/sqlite-storage.ts`  | `src/SqliteStorage.ts` |
+| `services/platform.ts`        | `src/Platform.ts`      |
+| `packlets/migrations/`        | `src/Migrations.ts`    |

body:
You're right on both counts, and the second one is the substantive hit — let me concede it precisely rather than hand-wave.

**The type-only imports hide a real dependency.** `Tags.ts` does `import { type IdentityManager } from './packlets/identity/identity-manager.ts'` and then declares the tag as `Context.Service<IdentityManagerService, IdentityManager>`. The *service type is the implementation class*. So `spaces` still depends on `identity`'s implementation — at the type level, structurally, and through the class's entire public surface. All I removed was the emitted `require`. My graph script then reports "acyclic" because it measures runtime edges, which makes it complicit: it certifies exactly the property the trick preserves. That's worse than a visible cycle, because it's a cycle nobody will notice.

**And grouping by kind is the wrong axis.** `Tags.ts` is "all the tags" for the same reason `Events.ts` is "all the events" — expedient, not principled. A reader looking for "what is the identity subsystem's contract" has to visit three files and filter each.

## What I'd propose

Subsystem contract modules, each owning its tags *and* the interfaces those tags are typed against, with the interfaces declared independently rather than aliased to a class:

```
src/
  Identity/
    contract.ts    -- IdentityManager, IdentityLifecycle, IdentityProvider (interfaces)
                   -- + their tags, + the identity lifecycle events
    internal/…     -- IdentityManagerImpl etc., which `implements` the contract
  Data/
    contract.ts    -- DataSpaceManager, SigningContext, the DataSpace contract, tags, events
    internal/…
```

The rule that makes it real: **a contract module may not import an implementation module, and the checker enforces that on type edges too, not just runtime ones.** Otherwise I've rebuilt the same hiding place with nicer names.

## What that costs, measured

The precedent is already in this package: `IdentityLifecycle` *is* a hand-written interface today, and its tag is typed against the interface, not the class. The others just never got the same treatment. Surfaces actually used by consumers:

| contract | members consumers touch |
| --- | --- |
| `IdentityLifecycle` | 2 — already an interface |
| `InvitationsManager` | 1 (`setInvitationHandlerFactory`) |
| `IdentityManager` | 5 (`identity`, `createIdentity`, `acceptIdentity`, `prepareIdentity`, `setEchoHost`) |
| `DataSpaceManager` | 11 |
| `IdentityProvider` / `SigningContextProvider` | already function types |

So four interfaces, ~19 members total. The transitive types they mention are cheap too: `DataSpace` is referenced in exactly **1** file outside `spaces` (and this PR already narrowed that one to a structural `ExportableSpace`), `SigningContext` in 3.

**The one that isn't cheap is `Identity`** — 18 files outside its module touch ~12 members (`identityKey`, `deviceKey`, `haloSpaceId`, `profileDocument`, `space`, `controlPipeline`, `authVerifier`, `stateUpdate`, `open`/`close`, …). That's an aggregate, not a service, and I don't think forcing it behind an interface buys anything; I'd leave it concrete and tier-1, where this PR already put it.

## On "existing places"

I looked. `@dxos/client-protocol` already has exactly this shape — `echo.ts`, `halo.ts`, `space.ts`, re-exported as `export type *`. But those are the **client-facing** contracts (what the app sees across the RPC boundary), and these are **host-internal** manager contracts. Putting host internals there would widen a published package's surface for an internal layering problem. I'd keep them in `client-services` unless you read that boundary differently — you may well.

## How do you want this sequenced?

1. **Follow-up PR.** Land this one on its structural merit (kernel extraction and the tier-1 leaves stand on their own and are not affected by this), and do contracts properly next, including teaching the checker about type edges. My preference — it's a design change that deserves its own diff rather than being appended to a 68-file one.
2. **In this PR.** I fold the contract modules in now; the diff grows and the whole thing re-reviews.
3. **Something else** — if the subsystem split you have in mind is coarser or finer than Identity/Data, say so and I'll work to that; the names above are mine and I'm not attached to them.

Either way I'll drop the "acyclic" claim from the PR description until the check actually measures what it claims to.

Correcting my previous reply: the fix I described is not what landed, because main moved underneath it.

`0005_rebuild_fts_text` rebuilt the full-text table with a `text` column in place of `snapshot`, and `FtsIndex.query` now reads `ftsIndex AS f` on **both** branches — the index stores the extracted text, so a term below the trigram minimum scans that column rather than another store. Pointing the unranked branch at `objectSnapshot` was right against the old code and wrong against this one; it failed every full-text test in the e2e suite with `no such column: f.snapshot`.

The live bug the merge exposed is that `buildFtsCondition` — the helper the compiler shares with the index — still named `f.snapshot` after that rename. Fixed in f3ae4a9b: the helper builds on `f.text`, and the compiler reads `ftsIndex` on both branches, matching `FtsIndex.query`. The e2e query suite forced to `sql` is back to 185 passed.

Confirmed and fixed in f3ae4a9b — this was real. `0008_normalized_ids` only does `ADD COLUMN` plus `CREATE INDEX`, `hasCompleteSnapshots()` counts missing snapshots and nothing else, and `reverseRef`'s cursor bump does not help here because `objectMeta` is written by the primary pass, whose cursors no migration resets. So an upgraded database kept `parentId`/`sourceId`/`targetId` NULL until each object next changed, and the compiled path silently omitted dependency, `child-of` and relation results for everything untouched.

Fixed with a backfill rather than a wider gate, since the gate would only delay the same missing data:

- `0009_backfill_normalized_ids` walks `objectMeta` in batches of 500 and fills the three columns for every row with a `parent`, `source` or `target` set.
- It derives them with `localEntityId`, the same function the indexing pass uses, so a backfilled row is indistinguishable from a rewritten one. That meant moving `localEntityId` into `entity-ids.ts` — importing it from the index would have made the migration module depend on the index that imports the migrations.
- As you noted, `NULL` is valid for a cross-space or non-entity reference, so rows are selected on the EID column being set rather than on the id column being NULL. The migration runs once, tracked in the migrations table, so that is idempotent.

Covered by a test in `entity-meta-index.test.ts` that inserts a pre-0008 row and a cross-space one: the local reference normalizes to its bare id, the cross-space one stays NULL. It fails without the migration and passes with it.

Doc claims in `SQL_QUERY_EXECUTION.md` corrected in the same commit, including your other thread's four items.
